summary: Metaxalone (Skelaxin) is a centrally acting skeletal muscle relaxant of the oxazolidinone class, indicated as an adjunct to rest, physical therapy, and other measures for the relief of discomforts associated with acute, painful musculoskeletal conditions in adults and children over 12 years of age. Its exact mechanism in humans has not been established but may be due to general central nervous system depression; it has no direct action on the contractile mechanism of striated muscle, the motor end plate, or the nerve fiber. The usual dose is one 800 mg tablet three to four times a day. Notable label safety concerns include the potential for hemolytic anemia and leukopenia, hepatotoxicity (jaundice, abnormal liver function studies), and rare anaphylactoid reactions. It is contraindicated in patients with known drug-induced hemolytic or other anemias, significantly impaired renal or hepatic function, and hypersensitivity, and it may enhance the effects of alcohol and other CNS depressants. Deaths have occurred with deliberate or accidental overdose, particularly in combination with antidepressants and alcohol.
indications: Adjunct to rest, physical therapy, and other measures for the relief of discomforts associated with acute, painful musculoskeletal conditions in adults and children over 12 years of age

dosage.d: 800 mg three to four times a day
dosage.n: Tablet is scored; a high-fat meal increases absorption

admin: Administer orally; the 800 mg tablet is scored
Food, especially a high-fat meal, significantly increases absorption and may enhance CNS depression; the elderly may be especially susceptible
May impair mental and physical abilities for hazardous tasks such as driving or operating machinery
Use as an adjunct to rest and physical therapy
Avoid concurrent alcohol and other CNS depressants
moa: The mechanism of action of metaxalone in humans has not been established but may be due to general central nervous system depression. Metaxalone has no direct action on the contractile mechanism of striated muscle, the motor end plate, or the nerve fiber, and is therefore classified as a centrally acting skeletal muscle relaxant.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to metaxalone or any tablet component
Known tendency to drug-induced, hemolytic, or other anemias
relative: Pre-existing liver damage (administer with great care and monitor)
Elderly patients (greater exposure and CNS susceptibility)
Concurrent use of alcohol or other CNS depressants
monitor: Serial liver function tests, especially with pre-existing liver damage
Complete blood count with repeated or prolonged use (leukopenia, hemolytic anemia)
Sedation / CNS depression, especially in the elderly

preg: Safe use has not been established with regard to possible adverse effects on fetal development. Use during pregnancy, or in women who may become pregnant, only when the potential benefits outweigh the possible hazards.
lact: It is not known whether metaxalone is secreted in human milk. Because many drugs are excreted in human milk, caution should be exercised, and nursing is discouraged during therapy.
renal: Metaxalone is contraindicated in significantly impaired renal function. The impact of renal disease on its pharmacokinetics has not been determined; use with caution.
hepatic: Metaxalone is contraindicated in significantly impaired hepatic function. It should be given with great care to patients with pre-existing liver damage, with serial liver function studies; jaundice and abnormal liver function tests have been reported.

major: Central nervous system depressants - alcohol, benzodiazepines, opioids, and tricyclic antidepressants - produce additive sedation; overdose deaths have been reported with antidepressants and alcohol
moderate: Other sedating or anticholinergic agents may add to drowsiness
minor: May produce a false-positive test for urinary glucose (Benedict's test) due to an unidentified reducing substance
interactions.food: A high-fat meal markedly increases absorption (Cmax and AUC) and may enhance CNS depression.
interactions.diagnostics: May cause a false-positive Benedict's (copper-reduction) test for glucosuria.

emergency: Severe sedation or respiratory depression (especially in overdose)

monitoring: Complete blood count with differential (with repeated use)
Signs of CNS depression / sedation, especially in the elderly and with concomitant CNS depressants
counsel: This medicine may cause drowsiness or dizziness; do not drive or operate machinery until you know how it affects you
Avoid alcohol and other sedating medicines
Report yellowing of the skin or eyes, unusual tiredness, paleness, or any signs of an allergic reaction
Continue rest and physical therapy - this medicine is an add-on treatment
Tell your doctor if you have kidney disease, liver disease, or a history of anemia
pk: Skeletal muscle relaxant effect after oral absorption
Peak plasma concentration about 3 hours after a 400 mg dose (fasted)
Dosed three to four times daily
Store at controlled room temperature 15-30 C (59-86 F)
pearls: Despite being a 'muscle relaxant,' it has no direct action on skeletal muscle - the effect is general CNS depression
A high-fat meal markedly boosts absorption - counsel patients on consistent administration relative to food
Bioavailability is higher in females and increases with age in the fasted state, so the elderly may show higher exposure and greater CNS susceptibility
Contraindicated in significant renal or hepatic impairment and in drug-induced or other anemias
Overdose deaths have occurred, especially in combination with antidepressants and alcohol
missed: Not specified in the label. General guidance: take a missed dose when you remember unless it is near the next scheduled dose, in which case skip it; do not take a double dose.
overdose: Deaths by deliberate or accidental overdose have occurred, particularly in combination with antidepressants and alcohol. Findings include progressive sedation, hypnosis, and respiratory failure. Treatment is gastric lavage and supportive therapy; consult a regional poison control center.
